summary: Defines optimizations to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for 6LoWPANs, such as IEEE 802.15.4 networks. These links make little use of multicast to save energy and may not follow normal IP subnet ideas. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny battery-powered gadgets cannot shout to everyone to save power. This memo gives them a quieter way to find neighbors.

questions: ipv6 neighbor discovery for low-power wireless
what is the address registration option
how does 6lowpan duplicate address detection work
subtitle: Trimming IPv6 Neighbor Discovery for battery-powered wireless nodes that sleep, lose links and cannot afford multicast.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery leans on multicast and assumes nodes are always awake on a single shared link, which suits Ethernet but wastes energy and often fails on lossy, low-power wireless networks.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts register their addresses with routers using a new Address Registration Option in unicast messages, routers keep those registrations instead of multicasting to find hosts, and border routers hand out prefixes and header compression contexts, with two new messages for duplicate address checks across multiple hops.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can sleep, multicast is almost eliminated, and the same prefixes work across a multihop network. RFC 6775 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944 and has itself been updated by RFC 8505, RFC 8929 and RFC 9010.

today: RFC 6775 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012 that updates RFC 4944. It has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 8505, RFC 8929 and RFC 9010, so check those for current behavior.

sections.title: Why Neighbor Discovery Needs Trimming
sections.content:
A 6LoWPAN (IPv6 over Low-power Wireless Personal Area Network, such as IEEE 802.15.4) is lossy, low-power, low-bit-rate and short-range, and many of its nodes sleep for long periods. Its links are asymmetric and non-transitive, so the idea of link-local scope really depends on radio reachability. The available link-layer payload is on the order of less than 100 bytes, which is why header compression is so useful.

Standard IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) fits this badly. A node multicasts to detect duplicate addresses and to find routers, routers multicast periodic advertisements, and address resolution uses multicast Neighbor Solicitations. All of that assumes nodes are mostly powered on and share one broadcast domain. RFC 6775 keeps the protocol but makes it quieter. Its optimisations are host-initiated interactions for sleeping hosts, no multicast address resolution for hosts, address registration in unicast messages, a new option to distribute header compression context, multihop distribution of prefix and context, and multihop duplicate address detection.

The scope is limited: it applies to LoWPANs where every node implements these optimisations in the same way. It updates RFC 4944 to specify their use.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal IPv6 is like a classroom where everyone shouts out names to find each other. In a field full of sleepy, tiny gadgets that is too loud and too tiring, so this memo gives them a quieter way.

sections.title: Roles, Topologies and Substitutable Features
sections.content:
The document names three kinds of node. A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) is any host or router. A 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) forwards packets and sends Router Advertisements, and exists only in route-over topologies. A 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) sits at the edge of the LoWPAN and is the authority for prefix propagation. In a mesh-under topology the mesh forwards at the link layer, so all hosts are one IP hop from the 6LBR and there are no 6LRs. In a route-over topology hosts are typically several IP hops from a 6LBR, reached through 6LRs.

The most important change is the host-to-router interaction, which is the same in both topologies. Multicast Neighbor Discovery is only used when a host needs an initial set of default routers or has to find new ones. Everything else is unicast and started by the host.

Two features are substitutable, meaning a routing protocol specification may replace them: multihop distribution of prefix and header compression context, and multihop duplicate address detection. An implementation MUST support them unless it supports such a substitute. The prefix and context features go together, so if one is substituted, both must be.
sections.plainLanguage: There are small gadgets, helper gadgets that pass messages along, and one boss gadget at the edge that knows the network's address book. The gadgets always talk to a helper in the same polite way, however far from the boss they are.

sections.title: New Options and Messages
sections.content:
The document defines three new Neighbor Discovery options and two new ICMPv6 messages.

The Address Registration Option (ARO, type 33) goes in unicast Neighbor Solicitations from hosts and in the answering Neighbor Advertisements. It carries a Status (0 in solicitations), a Registration Lifetime in units of 60 seconds, and the 64-bit EUI-64 of the interface, which lets a router tell the same node re-registering from a different node claiming the same address. Status 0 means success, 1 duplicate address, 2 Neighbor Cache full. A host MUST also include a Source Link-Layer Address Option, and the address being registered is the IPv6 source address of the solicitation.

The 6LoWPAN Context Option (6CO, type 34) carries a header compression context: a 4-bit Context Identifier (CID), a prefix of any length up to 128 bits, a Valid Lifetime in 60 second units and a C flag saying whether the context may be used for compression. Up to 16 6COs may be carried in one Router Advertisement.

The Authoritative Border Router Option (ABRO, type 35) carries a 32-bit version number, a Valid Lifetime and the IPv6 address of the 6LBR that originated the information. Routers that relay prefixes and contexts use the version number so that older information never overrides newer.

The Duplicate Address Request (DAR, ICMPv6 type 157) and Duplicate Address Confirmation (DAC, type 158) share one format that inlines the ARO fields plus the registered address. They are new messages because they are forwarded across hops, so they cannot satisfy the hop limit 255 check of Neighbor Discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds some new little forms. One form says here is my name and how long to remember me. One carries shorthand codes that shrink messages. One says which boss gadget wrote the address book and which edition it is.

sections.title: How a Host Behaves
sections.content:
A host forms its link-local address from its EUI-64 and sends a Router Solicitation to the all-routers multicast address with a Source Link-Layer Address Option, so the router can answer by unicast. It sends up to 3 solicitations at least 10 seconds apart, then backs off exponentially, never waiting longer than 60 seconds between tries. A host MUST NOT multicast a Neighbor Solicitation, and it does not join the solicited-node multicast address.

For an address not derived from an EUI-64, the M flag in the Router Advertisement decides the method. If M is set, DHCPv6 MUST be used. If it is clear, the host can choose another way, and duplicate detection happens as part of registration. A host ignores a Prefix Information Option with the on-link flag set. Once an address is configured, the host registers it by unicasting a Neighbor Solicitation with an ARO to one or more default routers, and SHOULD try more than one router for robustness. It renews well before the Registration Lifetime ends, and de-registers by sending a lifetime of 0.

Registration can be combined with Neighbor Unreachability Detection, since both are unicast solicitations. If the answer carries Status 1, the host MUST NOT use that address. If it carries Status 2, the host SHOULD drop that router and try another. Because every exchange is started by the host, it can sleep: it picks a Registration Lifetime longer than its sleep time, refreshes registrations that would expire before the next wakeup, and only multicasts again if its old routers have become unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: A sleepy gadget wakes up, quietly asks a nearby helper to remember its name for a while, and goes back to sleep. If the helper says that name is taken, it picks a new one.

sections.title: How Routers Keep Track of Hosts
sections.content:
Routers no longer multicast to find hosts. They keep a Neighbor Cache Entry for every registered address, so for 6LoWPAN routers the Neighbor Cache behaves less like a cache and more like a registry of attached hosts. There are three types of entry: garbage-collectible (normal RFC 4861 rules), registered (kept until the registered lifetime ends or the host de-registers) and tentative (short-lived, usually turned into registered). Routers SHOULD NOT garbage collect registered entries, and one marked unreachable by NUD is kept until its lifetime expires.

When a Neighbor Solicitation with an ARO arrives, the router checks for a duplicate. It is not one if no entry exists for the source address, or an entry exists with the same EUI-64. For a duplicate, the router answers with Status 1 and changes nothing. If the cache is full, it answers with Status 2. Otherwise it creates or updates the entry, records the lifetime and EUI-64, and replies with a copy of the ARO with Status 0. A lifetime of 0 deletes the entry. Errors go to the link-local address derived from the EUI-64 in the ARO, not to the source address, because of a possible risk of link-layer address collision.

Routers always answer a Router Solicitation by unicast and need not send periodic advertisements, since hosts ask before lifetimes expire. A router MUST NOT set the on-link flag in prefix options, and SHOULD NOT send Redirect messages in route-over topologies, because radio propagation means it cannot know whether one host can reach another directly.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper gadgets keep a guest book. When a gadget signs in, the helper writes down its name and how long to keep the entry. If someone else tries to sign in with the same name, the helper says no.

sections.title: Border Routers and the Multihop Features
sections.content:
A 6LBR gets the LoWPAN's prefixes by manual configuration or DHCPv6 prefix delegation, or generates a Unique Local Address prefix if the LoWPAN is isolated. If header compression context is used, the 6LBR manages the Context Identifiers and advertises one 6CO per context. Context must be consistent everywhere, so several 6LBRs MUST be configured with the same context and CIDs. New context SHOULD first be sent with the C flag clear, so every node can decompress with it, and only later with C set so it can be used to compress. A context SHOULD keep being sent with C clear for at least 300 seconds (MIN_CONTEXT_CHANGE_DELAY) before it is dropped or reused with a different prefix.

In a route-over network the substitutable multihop prefix and context distribution works through Router Advertisements between routers. The 6LBR puts an ABRO in each one and increases its version whenever the prefixes or contexts change. A router ignores an advertisement without an ABRO, ignores one with a lower version than it has stored for that 6LBR, and keeps each 6LBR's information together with that 6LBR's ABRO.

The substitutable multihop duplicate address detection lets a 6LR check an address against the 6LBR. The 6LR creates a tentative entry, unicasts a DAR to a 6LBR, and the 6LBR looks the address up in its DAD table. If the address is known with a different EUI-64 it answers with a DAC with Status 1. Otherwise it records the entry and answers with Status 0. When the DAC arrives the 6LR makes its entry registered and tells the host with a Neighbor Advertisement. Tentative entries time out after 20 seconds, and DARs are sent with a hop limit of 64. Because the hop limit check cannot apply, routers MUST NOT change the Neighbor Cache on a DAR, and only on a DAC when it matches a tentative entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss gadget writes the address book and numbers each edition. Helpers only believe the newest edition. Before a helper lets a gadget use a new name, it phones the boss to check nobody else already has it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) and address autoconfiguration (RFC 4862) apply, along with the threat discussion in RFC 3756. The RFC assumes the link layer is sufficiently protected, for instance by MAC-sublayer cryptography, so the threat model is no different from that of RFC 4861. Link-layer security protocols for 6LoWPAN are out of scope.

There is one slight change. Because the M flag disables stateless autoconfiguration for non-EUI-64 addresses, a rogue router can force DHCP-only use for short addresses, rather than only adding DHCP as an option.

The multihop DAD messages are forwarded, so the hop limit 255 check does not apply and in principle any node on the Internet could send them. The RFC contains this by requiring routers never to modify a Neighbor Cache Entry because of such messages (except by a matching DAC for a tentative entry), and to discard them unless they arrive on an interface explicitly configured for these optimisations. Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971) could be used between hosts and routers because the address being registered is the source address of the solicitation, but applying it between routers is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo assumes the gadgets already talk over a locked radio channel. It adds a rule that helpers must not change their guest books just because a far-away message says so.

items.title: Garbage-collectible
items.text: Follows the normal RFC 4861 rules and may be removed when memory is low.

items.text: Has an explicit lifetime and is kept until it expires or the host de-registers.

items.title: Tentative
items.text: Temporary with a short lifetime; usually becomes a Registered entry.
